opus-5.5.text:
I have pretty mixed feelings about it, honestly.

On one hand, I understand why companies do it. Building a frontier model now is a massive collective effort: hundreds of people on data, infrastructure, evaluation, safety, post-training. It's genuinely hard to say who "deserves" the credit, and a team byline reflects that the work really is a team product. There's also a practical side. These people are extremely valuable, and every name on a paper is basically a recruiting target for competitors. So I get the logic, both the idealistic version and the cynical one.

But I think something important gets lost. Research has always been driven by individuals with specific ideas and specific taste. When you look back at the history of deep learning, you remember ResNet, the Transformer, and you remember the people behind them. That attribution isn't just vanity. It's how the community builds trust, how young researchers learn whose thinking to follow, and how people build a career and a reputation that's portable, that belongs to them and not to an employer.

When everything becomes "the X team," the researcher becomes a bit more like a component in a machine. For senior people who already have their reputation, maybe that's fine. For a PhD student or an early-career researcher deciding whether to go to industry or academia, it's a real cost. You might do the most important work of your life and nobody outside will ever know it was you.

I also worry about the broader effect on science. A blog post with a team byline is usually not really a paper. It's closer to a product announcement. There's less detail, less reproducibility, less accountability. Science works when someone stands behind a claim with their name. So the anonymous byline and the move away from open publishing are, I think, two sides of the same trend: AI research turning from science into industry.

That's part of why I still care a lot about academia and open research. Somebody needs to keep doing work where the ideas are public, the methods are shared, and the people who had the ideas get recognized for them. I don't think the industry model is wrong for what it's trying to do. I just don't think it should be the only model.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts industry research with academia and open research, but does not clearly say team bylines disrupt exchange between academia and industry.

r002.rationale: It describes research as driven by ideas and taste, but does not characterize it as motivated by love of exploration or contrast that motive with commercial returns.

r003.rationale: It says individual attribution builds trust, guides young researchers, and supports careers, but does not clearly identify credit assignment as a mechanism behind academic progress over past decades.

fable-5.1.text:
I have complicated feelings about it, honestly. I understand why companies do it. When you have hundreds of people contributing to a system like Gemini or GPT, it genuinely becomes hard to draw a line and say these twenty people are the authors and these other hundred are not. Everything is so entangled now, from data to infrastructure to pretraining to post-training, that attributing credit the way we do in academia almost stops making sense. And there's also a practical side: companies don't want their best people to be visible targets for recruiters, and they want the product to be the brand, not the individual.

But I think something real is lost. Science has always run on individual reputation and individual accountability. When I read a paper, I know who did it, I can follow that person's trajectory, I can see how their thinking evolved, and young researchers can look up to specific people and say, I want to do work like that. If everything becomes "the team," then for a PhD student or a junior researcher inside those labs, your contribution just disappears into a collective. That's hard for career development, and it's hard for the field, because we lose the ability to trace where ideas actually came from.

The other thing that bothers me is that this trend coincides with the shift from papers to blog posts and technical reports. So not only do we lose the names, we also lose the details. You get a nice write-up with benchmark numbers, but you don't know what was really done, and you can't ask the person who did it. It makes the whole thing less reproducible and, frankly, less like science and more like product marketing.

I don't think the answer is going back to five-author papers. Maybe it's something like how large physics collaborations handle it, where there's a long author list and a clear contribution statement. The key is that people should still be able to get credit for their ideas. In academia we're in a slightly different position: we can still do work where it's very clear who did what, and I think that's actually one of the advantages of being in a university right now. You can own your ideas, you can publish openly, and the community can see you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lost individual credit and the advantages of university research, but does not say team bylines disrupt exchange between academia and industry.

r002.rationale: It discusses science, ideas, and career development, but does not characterize research as driven by love of exploration rather than commercial returns.

r003.rationale: It says science has long relied on individual reputation and accountability, and argues that clear attribution lets people trace ideas and receive credit—identifying credit assignment as a longstanding support for academic work.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things we should separate: recognizing that research is a team effort, and making the individuals who contributed invisible. You can acknowledge the team without removing people’s names.

For a researcher, especially someone early in their career, attribution matters. It’s how other people understand what you’ve worked on and what you contributed. If the only name on the work is the organization’s, the organization builds its reputation, but it becomes harder for the individual to build theirs.

Of course, with a large project, a short author list may not capture everyone’s contribution either. But that’s a reason to provide better attribution—perhaps a contribution statement or a detailed credits section. I’d like to see the team recognized and the people recognized. Those shouldn’t be competing goals.

r001.rationale: The response discusses individual attribution and organizational reputation, but does not say team-name bylines disrupt exchange between academia and industry.

r002.rationale: It does not describe research as driven by exploration or love of discovery rather than commercial returns.

r003.rationale: It supports clearer attribution, but does not identify credit assignment as a mechanism that has supported academic progress over past decades.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things we should separate: giving credit to a team and making individual contributions invisible. Research is increasingly collaborative, so a team byline can make sense. But that doesn’t mean you have to remove the names of the people who did the work. You can have both.

For a company, the team name builds the company’s brand. For an individual researcher, especially someone early in their career, having their name attached to their work is how they build a reputation. There’s a real asymmetry there. The organization already has visibility; the individual may not.

And authorship is also about accountability. If I read something interesting, I want to know who worked on it, who I can ask questions, who deserves credit. A generic byline makes that harder.

I wouldn’t assume every team byline has a bad motivation. Sometimes contributions are genuinely difficult to separate. But my preference is pretty simple: celebrate the team, and still make the people and their contributions visible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visibility and credit for individual researchers, but does not connect team bylines to disruption of exchange between academia and industry.

r002.rationale: It does not describe research as driven by exploration or distinguish that motivation from commercial returns.

r003.rationale: It says identifying contributors helps with credit and accountability, but does not say that clear credit assignment has supported academic progress over past decades.
